extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / experimental physicists studying fluid motion and resistance (readers of Newton's Principia)
extracted.subtask_description: Theoretical and experimental rules for determining fluid efflux, pressures, and the resistance experienced by spherical bodies moving in fluids, together with recommended experimental methods (pendulum decay) and scaling laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efflux velocity equals free-fall velocity from same head (Torricelli law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Est igitur velocitas quacum aqua exit e foramine, ad velocitatem quam aqua cadens, & tempore T cadendo describens spatium S acquireret, ut altitudo aquæ foramini perpendiculariter incumbens, ad medium proportionale inter altitudinem illam duplicatam & spatium illud S...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Velocity of efflux from an orifice is related to the velocity a body would acquire by falling through a height determined by the head of water; use the geometric proportionalities given (medium proportional between twice the head and the fall S) when comparing efflux and free-fall velocities. Note caveat: applies to very fluid (ideal) fluids; coarser/viscous fluids efflux more slowly than this rule predicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of efflux ∝ area/space available for flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitas aquæ dato tempore defluentis erit ut amplitudo foraminis per quod defluit; hoc est, si Globus tollatur, ut canalis orificium: sin Globus adsit, ut spatium undique inter Globum & canalem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The volumetric amount of fluid passing per time is proportional to the effective cross-sectional area available (or the gap between an inserted sphere and canal). Use this when comparing cases with obstructions (globe present) versus unobstructed orifice. Adjust for reduced flow in non-ideal (thicker) fluids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oblique efflux traces a parabola with latus rectum equal to head
rubrics_metrics.description: Si aqua egrediatur oblique per canalem ... describet in spatiis non resistentibus Parabolam cujus latus rectum est altitudo aquæ in vase supra canalis orificium, & cujus diameter horizonti perpendicularis ab orificio illo ducitur...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When fluid exits obliquely into a medium without resistance, its trajectory is a parabola. The geometric parameters are given: latus rectum equals the vertical head above the orifice; ordinates are parallel to the canal axis. Useful for predicting jet shape in ideal (nonresisting) surroundings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local pressure loss at an outlet equals weight of a column of fluid of base equal to the outlet and height equal to head above outlet
rubrics_metrics.description: Vas sustinebit pondus aquæ totius, non obstante effluxu, sed latus vasis de quo effluit non sustinebit pressionem illam omnem. Tolletur enim pressio partis illius ubi perforatur: quæ quidem pressio æqualis est ponderi columnæ aquæ, cujus basis foramini æquatur & altitudo eadem est quæ aquæ totius supra foramen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When fluid flows out through an opening in a side wall, the overall container still supports the total weight vertically, but the wall at the outlet loses the pressure corresponding to the column of fluid that would sit above the opening. Use this to compute pressure distribution changes due to an orifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action–reaction equivalence for efflux and obstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Actio & reactio aquæ per motus Legem tertiam æquantur inter se, & in plagas contrarias diriguntur. Actio Globi in aquam descendentem, ad ejus descensum impediendum, in superiora dirigitur, & est ut descendendi motus impeditus... & propterea actio contraria aquæ in Globum æqualis est vi quæ motum eundem vel tollere vel generare possit, hoc est ponderi columnæ aquæ, quæ Globo perpendiculariter imminet & cujus altitudo est RS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The resisting force exerted on an obstacle by moving fluid equals the reactive force the obstacle exerts on the fluid; quantitatively, here it is equated to the weight of a fluid column whose base equals the cross-section of the globe and whose height is the relevant head (RS). Apply Newton's third law to relate prevented fluid descent to force on the body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance of a sphere relates to weight of displaced column (geometric formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vim aquæ decurrentis sustinet ponderi illi æqualem. ... action contraria aquæ in Globum æqualis est vi quæ motum eundem vel tollere vel generare possit, hoc est ponderi columnæ aquæ, quæ Globo perpendiculariter imminet & cujus altitudo est RS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute resistance by comparing to the weight of a column of fluid whose base equals the projected area (cylindrical base equal to sphere cross-section) and height equals the fluid head designated (RS). This gives a geometric/ hydrostatic estimate of resistance for idealized situations; adjust for viscosity and flow details in real fluids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entrainment principle (Lemma IV & Prop. XXXIX)
rubrics_metrics.description: Partes Fluidi inclusi, æqualiter participando motum vasis, quiescent inter se. ... Fluidum omne quod motu progressivo accelerato fertur, & cujus partes inter se quiescunt, solida quæcunque ejusdem densitatis inclusa ... rapit secum, & una moveri cogit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a homogeneous fluid is imparted a progressive accelerated motion whose parts remain at rest relative to each other, then solids of the same density suspended in it will be carried along with the fluid. Use this to reason about entrainment/transport of neutrally buoyant bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental method: measure resistance from pendulum amplitude decay
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimenta usus sumus oscillantium pendulorum, eo quod eorum motus facilius & accuratius observari & mensurari possint. ... numerabam oscillationes quibus pendulum quartam motus sui partem amitteret ... differentia arcuum ... dividantur per numerum oscillationum ... deducantur A, B, C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To determine the law of resistance, observe successive amplitudes (first descent arc and last ascent arc) and count oscillations until a given fraction of motion is lost; compute differences in arcs per oscillation and fit them to a series in powers of velocity (A·V + B·V^{3/2} + C·V^2). Solve linear systems from multiple experiments with differing maximum velocities to extract coefficients A, B, C. Account for filament (suspension) resistance and vessel confinement effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical decomposition of resistive loss: A·V + B·V^{3/2} + C·V^2
rubrics_metrics.description: Fingamus quod differentia arcuum sit AV + BV^{3/2} + CV^2. ... ex his ... fit A = 0,0002097, B = 0,0008955 & C = 0,0030298 (example numerical solution) ... differentia arcuum ut 0,0002097V + 0,0008955V^{3/2} + 0,0030298V^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model the decrement of oscillation amplitude per oscillation as a sum of terms proportional to V, V^{3/2} and V^2. Use measurements at several velocities to solve for coefficients. The V^2 term corresponds to resistance roughly quadratic in velocity (dominant at higher speeds); lower-order terms may arise from other effects (filament drag, flow separation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance scales approximately with square of diameter for similar conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Resistentiarum partes illæ quæ sunt (paribus Globis) ut quadrata velocitatum, sunt etiam (paribus velocitatibus) ut quadrata diametrorum Globorum; & propterea ... resistentia Globi ... haud multum per infinitam aeris divisionem & subtiliationem diminui potest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For geometrically similar spheres at comparable velocities, the resistance tends to be proportional to the square of their diameters (i.e., cross-sectional area scaling). Use this scaling when extrapolating between sizes, while noting deviations due to filament drag or confinement and that exact exponent may vary with flow regime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance of medium ≈ proportional to its density (for many fluids)
rubrics_metrics.description: Igitur resistentia ... partem illa sola quæ est in duplicata ratione velocitatis ... erit ad vim quæ totum corporis motum ... ut densitas Medii ad densitatem corporis quamproxime. ... ex jam descriptis satis liquet resistentiam corporum celeriter motorum densitati Fluidorum in quibus moventur proportionalem esse quamproxime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing different fluids under similar flow regimes, the part of resistance proportional to velocity squared is approximately proportional to the fluid density. Experiments (mercury vs water) support approximate proportionality of resistance to fluid density. Beware that viscosity/tenacity causes deviations for fluids of same density.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viscosity/tenacity and confinement effects: departures from ideal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Nam si aqua ex partibus crassioribus constet, hæc tardius effluet quam pro ratione superius assignata, præsertim si foramen angustum sit ... Fluida tenaciora pari densitate proculdubio magis resistunt quam liquidiora ... in vasis nimis angustiis motum aquæ cedentis præ angustia sua nimis impediebat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect deviations from ideal (inviscid) predictions when the fluid has significant viscosity or when the experimental vessel/channel is too narrow relative to the body, which increases resistance beyond the simple scaling laws. Design experiments with sufficiently large vessels and bodies to minimize confinement; note that colder/heavier oils resist more than warm water despite similar density.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit and asymptotic reasoning: use large-body limit to infer resistance law
rubrics_metrics.description: In Fluido quocunque dato inveniatur resistentia ultima solidi specie dati, cujus magnitudo in infinitum augetur. ... ergo ex resistentia solidi aucti in Medio non subtiliato, dabitur per proportionem superiorem resistentia solidi non aucti in Medio subtiliato.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To infer the ultimate (asymptotic) resistance behavior, consider increasing the solid's size to infinity (or compare limits) and use proportional reasoning (e.g., relation between increased solid size and resistance). This gives constraints on how resistance changes with changes in fluid particle size and on the limiting dependence (approximate area scaling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental recommendations and corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Optarim itaque ... ut experimenta cum Globis & pluribus & majoribus & magis accuratis tentarentur. ... de calculo accurato in experimento non satis accurato minime sollicitus. ... Debebit tamen resistentia tam in aere quam in aqua, si velocitas per gradus in infinitum augeatur, augeri tandem in ratione paulo plusquam duplicata, propterea quod ... corpora longe velocissima spatium a tergo relinquent vacuum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: use multiple spheres of different sizes (preferably geometrically scaled), larger vessels to avoid confinement, account and correct for suspension filament drag, and repeat experiments in varied fluids (including denser/less dense) and temperatures. Expect higher-speed bodies to show resistance slightly greater than quadratic due to wake effects (vacuum left behind).
